articles.title: Carlos Bardem: "Con Guy Ritchie, yo no rodé nunca una frase que estuviera en el guion"
articles.standfirst: El actor presenta 'En la zona gris', un thriller lleno de acción dirigido por Guy Ritchie
articles.summary: El actor presenta 'En la zona gris', un thriller lleno de acción dirigido por Guy Ritchie
articles.body: Carlos Bardem protagoniza 'En la zona gris', la nueva película de Guy Ritchie, un thriller de acción en el que interpreta a Manny Salazar, un multimillonario que se convierte en el objetivo de un grupo de criminales que pretende arrebatarle mil millones de dólares. La cinta, rodada en 2023, cuenta con un reparto internacional encabezado por Jake Gyllenhaal, Henry Cavill, Eiza González y Rosamund Pike y combina acción, humor y los diálogos característicos del cine de Ritchie. La película llega ahora a España después de varios retrasos en su distribución. Con motivo de su estreno, hablamos con Carlos Bardem sobre su experiencia trabajando con Guy Ritchie y sobre el particular método del director británico, pero también sobre su nueva novela, 'Triángulo', la violencia verbal, su compromiso con distintas causas sociales y su relación con el Atlético de Madrid y el fútbol moderno. En 'En la zona gris' interpretas a Manny Salazar, un multimillonario al que quieren arrebatar mil millones de dólares. ¿Qué te atrajo de él? Lo primero que considero siempre es el guion. Lo leí y me pareció muy divertido, una película de Guy Ritchie, con acción y diálogos llenos de humor. Además, estaba la posibilidad de trabajar con Ritchie y con un casting como el de esta película, con Henry Cavill, Eiza González, Rosamund Pike... Todo eso hacía un paquete muy atractivo para interpretar a Manny Salazar. ¿Qué tiene Guy Ritchie como director que hace que un actor acepte que el guion pueda cambiar prácticamente delante de sus ojos? La película me llegó como una oferta directa a través de mis agentes. Tenía el guion dos meses y medio antes y, como la rodamos en inglés, me puse a trabajarlo mucho. Cuando llegué a los fittings, empecé a cruzarme con gente del equipo que me decía que Guy lo cambiaba todo. Me empecé a preocupar cuando me dijeron que Guy Ritchie lo cambiaba todo. Y efectivamente, Con Guy Ritchie, yo no rodé nunca una frase que estuviera en el guion que había estudiado durante dos meses y medio. Él viaja con guionistas, es coguionista y va cambiando las cosas en función de lo que ha rodado. Esta flexibilidad se la permite trabajar desde sus primeras películas con un grupo muy reducido de personas, su "gang", que se entiende con mirarse. Yo como actor lo viví con mucho susto inicialmente, porque me daban, con suerte, las escenas la noche anterior, muchas veces en el tráiler de maquillaje. Yo le decía: 'Oiga Mr. Ritchie, yo me manejo con el inglés pero entenderá usted que estos cambios... Y me decía: 'No te preocupes que lo estás haciendo muy bien'. Pero vi que la cosa funcionaba y que todos los cambios que hacía mejoraban lo que había sobre papel. Una vez que entendí el juego, descubrí que lo que Guy exige a los actores es estar muy presentes, abiertos, flexibles y conectados con lo que están haciendo. Y acabó siendo uno de los rodajes más divertidos en los que he estado nunca. ¿Qué descubriste de ti como actor trabajando con Guy Ritchie que no esperabas descubrir? Yo ya con la edad que tengo, pues ya yo me tengo más o menos identificado, pero sí me alegró ver que era capaz de de asumir y abrazar ese reto. De rodar en un idioma que no es el mío, en una película en la que la gente habla mucho, hay unas unas parrafadas llenas de ironía, de doble sentidos... Todos nos pisábamos, eran réplicas constantes y me agradó ver que era capaz de hacerlo, que el resultado estaba bien y que el director no me despedía, me decía: 'Vuelva usted al día siguiente'. La película se rodó en 2023 y llega ahora a España, después de varios retrasos y cambios en su distribución. ¿En algún momento pensaste que se había quedado en un cajón? Yo contaba con que saldría porque es una película de Guy Ritchie y tiene estrellas muy conocidas de Hollywood. Pero sí, es una película que estuvo un tiempo metida en un cajón por problemas. Los detalles se me escapan, entre la productora, las distribuidoras y demás. En octubre publicas 'Triángulo', una novela sobre deseo, masculinidad y una fosa común de la Guerra Civil. ¿Qué querías explorar esta vez como escritor? Yo escribo para mí, para comprender cosas. Siempre cito a Borges, que decía que escribir es una manera de leer más profundamente. La novela empieza explorando la relación entre la masculinidad y las nuevas feminidades, pero, como ocurre en las buenas películas y los buenos libros, aparecen otros temas. En este caso, la memoria histórica y, fundamentalmente, la violencia crónica contra las mujeres. También es una llamada de atención contra la tibieza. En la 'Divina Comedia', Dante sitúa antes de la entrada al infierno a los tibios, los que no toman partido y se ponen de perfil pensando que a ellos nunca les va a pasar nada. Vivimos unos tiempos en los que creo que no hay que ponerse de perfil y en los que las torres de marfil no van a funcionar. Hace unos meses dijiste que la violencia verbal puede ser la antesala de la violencia física. Ahora tenemos los ejemplos de lo ocurrido en Oviedo, lo que está ocurriendo en Ceuta... ¿Qué estamos haciendo mal como sociedad? Es un tema muy complejo, pero hay una cosa que está clara: la violencia verbal siempre precede o es la antesala de la violencia física. Siempre se empieza por el insulto, por denigrar, por deshumanizar. Creo que vivimos un momento muy complejo y que la diferencia ahora es que quienes odian, gritan y deshumanizan tienen un altavoz muy potente y llegan a mucha gente. Creo que quienes no somos machistas, racistas, homófobos o fascistas tenemos que enfrentarnos a esos discursos de odio con contundencia, denunciarlos y demostrarles que somos más. Creo que esa es la única esperanza que tenemos como sociedad. Siempre has sido muy activo en causas sociales, desde la defensa del pueblo saharaui, pasando por Palestina y hasta cuestiones medioambientales. ¿Qué hace que una causa te lleve a implicarte públicamente y a asumir el coste de posicionarte? Creo que la implicación con las causas siempre tiene que ver con la negación de derechos humanos elementales. Yo apoyaré a colectivos y personas que estén siendo oprimidos y a quienes se nieguen derechos básicos, dignidad, igualdad, representación política o voz. Cuando tienes un altavoz, creo que no solo tienes el derecho, sino también la obligación de utilizarlo para denunciar lo que consideras injusto. ¿Te sorprende que posicionarse a favor de derechos humanos se perciba como izquierda cuando debería estar por encima de ideología? Creo que el auge de la extrema derecha y de los fascismos se basa en romper consensos básicos, como la igualdad entre hombres y mujeres. El feminismo no consiste en poner a las mujeres por encima de los hombres, sino en garantizar la igualdad. Eso debería ser un derecho básico, independientemente del sexo. También estamos viendo la criminalización de la inmigración. Incluso hay personas de izquierda que empiezan a justificar la inmigración porque los inmigrantes hacen determinados trabajos o porque son necesarios para las pensiones. Eso puede ser cierto, pero no debería ser la causa para dar un trato humanitario a una persona. Hay que hacerlo porque es un ser humano. Has dicho que te preocuparía más callarte por miedo que pagar un peaje por opinar. ¿Has pagado alguna vez ese peaje? Supongo que sí, o sé que sí, pero no me lo voy a beber. Yo no vengo aquí a cantar tangos ni a victimizarme. Cada uno tenemos una relación con nuestro estar en el mundo. Yo necesito sentir que, de alguna manera, contribuyo a lo que creo que es justo y hago lo que puedo. Muy futbolero y socio del Atlético. ¿Sigues viendo fútbol con la misma pasión? ¿Qué significa para ti el Atleti? El Atleti para mí significa lo que ha significado siempre: rebeldía. Soy de Madrid y, cuando era pequeño, iba al colegio y todos los niños eran del Madrid, salvo uno o dos que éramos del Atleti. Me crié con la sensación de que para ser del Madrid valía casi todo el mundo y que para ser del Atleti había que tener una manera muy especial. Has sido muy crítico con la transformación del fútbol en un negocio. ¿Cómo ves ese proceso? Odio eterno al fútbol moderno. Yo no soy un ingenuo. Entiendo que el fútbol siempre ha sido un negocio y que es un espectáculo, pero El fútbol cada vez tiene menos de competición y más de espectáculo guionizado. Creo que la monetización de todo está apartando a las aficiones. Los precios de las entradas y de las camisetas son una muestra. Tiene que ver también con la gentrificación: nuestras ciudades, los campos de fútbol y las competiciones se están convirtiendo en parques temáticos para turistas con dinero. Creo que se está perdiendo algo muy importante del fútbol, que es la pertenencia y la relación con un equipo y una afición. Has defendido que los futbolistas deberían posicionarse socialmente por el altavoz que tienen. Ahora tenemos el ejemplo de Borja Iglesias... ¿Los ves más implicados que antes? Y mira la que le ha caído... No se implican. Estadísticamente es imposible que no haya futbolistas gays y ninguno sale a decirlo. Mueven tal cantidad de dinero que entiendo que el negocio prima y que hay temas que pueden resultar incómodos para los patrocinadores. Cuando hay un colectivo en el que es imposible estadísticamente que no haya cierto tipo de personas y esas personas nunca se las ve, no tienen voz o están condenadas a callarse, creo que eso es significativo. Acabo de hacer una película en Argentina que habla de esto, 'No lo grites'. Interpreto a un agente de futbolistas y la película va de unos agentes que descubren a un niño que puede ser el próximo Maradona o Messi, pero el niño es gay. La duda es qué hacer con él: cumplir su sueño, pero pudiendo destrozarle la vida si tiene que ocultar quién es. Le preguntamos a la IA qué pregunta te haría si solo pudiera hacerte una y nos dijo esto: ¿En qué momento la ficción deja de ser un entretenimiento y se convierte en la herramienta más eficaz para despertar la conciencia política de un país? Buena pregunta de la inteligencia artificial que no es inteligencia ni es artificial, pero eso es otro debate. Los seres humanos necesitamos relatos para vivir. Construimos una memoria personal que nos permite tener un pasado y proyectarnos hacia un futuro, y las sociedades hacen lo mismo. Creo que la ficción es una manera de crear esa conversación: quiénes somos, de dónde venimos y hacia dónde vamos, y de llamar a la reflexión y a la emoción. Cuando actúo soy una pieza al servicio de una narrativa ajena, mientras que cuando escribo soy el dueño de esa narrativa. Yo siempre digo que yo no escribo para dar respuestas. No creo que esa sea la misión de la cultura. La cultura tiene que sembrar preguntas, sembrar dudas, cuestionar y luego que cada uno saque sus respuestas. Después de la película y la novela, ¿qué viene? Voy a estrenar una comedia de terror de Kiko Prada, 'Tránsito', en el Festival Isla Calavera de Tenerife en otoño. También está mi participación en la serie 'Atasco' y en 'Chiquito El Grande', una serie sobre Chiquito de la Calzada. Además, estoy escribiendo una novela nueva. Siempre estoy escribiendo.

articles.title: 'American Idol' ditches Hollywood for Georgia after two decades as California loses another production
articles.summary: "American Idol" is relocating from Hollywood to an Atlanta-area studio complex as Georgia's tax incentives and infrastructure lure major productions.
articles.body: "American Idol" is ditching Hollywood for Georgia amid renewed concerns about California’s competitiveness. On Wednesday, Fremantle, the production company behind ABC's long-running singing competition, confirmed the relocation to Fox News Digital. The company is reportedly in final discussions with an Atlanta-area studio complex, according to Deadline. Longtime fans and viewers of the show were quick to react on social media. "'You’re going to…Atlanta!' Just doesn’t have that same ring to it," one user wrote on X. "Another one bites the dust LA. Sad!" another added. "So much for those 'hollyweird' tax breaks eh?" one person quipped. NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE' "LOL !!! Another production Hollywood GETTING THE HELL OUT OF CALIFORNIA ! AFTER 25 YEARS BYEEEEE GAVIN NEWSOM American Idol is OUT OF CALI," another wrote. While the move marks a significant change for a series long associated with Hollywood, Lisa Cusack, president of the Don’t L.A. My Burbank PAC, said the relocation should be a warning to California officials. "The issue is that Georgia offers generous incentives for reality TV shows, while California often leaves them behind," Cusack told Fox News Digital. "For example, Nick Schultz’s entertainment tax credit bill, AB 2319, specifically excludes unscripted programming." "Now Georgia has a lot of the same infrastructure as Hollywood, and offers a less expensive, more family-friendly quality of life," she continued. "There’s very little keeping even Hollywood business in California anymore. This should serve as a five-shot-espresso wake-up call to Rob Bonta to settle with Paramount and not make things worse." Last month, Paramount CEO David Ellison threatened to relocate the company’s headquarters to a more business-friendly state such as Georgia, Tennessee or Texas if California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is leading 11 other states in an effort to block Paramount's $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), did not negotiate a settlement by Oct. 1. As Puck News reported, Ellison could move Paramount — and potentially Warner Bros. Discovery if he ultimately merges the companies — out of California "regardless of the eventual outcome of the case." Ellison has even developed a five-year plan that would relocate the vast majority of jobs out of the state while still maintaining a footprint in Hollywood. On Wednesday, TMZ reported that the Los Angeles Mayor's Office and the California Attorney General's Office were told Paramount would announce Tuesday that it was leaving California. No such announcement had been made as of Wednesday. "I tried to warn you," Spencer Pratt wrote on X following the TMZ news. "LA is getting absolutely decimated by the insane communist wackos running California. Bob Bonta’s jihad against Paramount is a death blow. What a corrupt piece of s---." According to Deadline, Georgia has become one of the country’s most competitive production hubs by offering a 20% base film and television tax credit, with a potential 10% promotional uplift for qualifying projects. The state’s official guidelines list television series among eligible productions and require at least $500,000 in qualified Georgia spending. Stephen Weizenecker, a partner at Barnes & Thornburg in Georgia, said there are three pillars to analyze when deciding whether to film in California or Georgia. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "Physical infrastructure is equally critical. A show like 'American Idol' requires massive sound stages, specialized equipment for elaborate performance sets, live-audience capacity, and proximity to rehearsal spaces, wardrobe, and production offices," said Weizenecker, who has had a direct role in developing Georgia's entertainment tax incentive framework and spent over two decades advising productions on filming all across the world. "Georgia now offers purpose-built studio campuses — including Tyler Perry Studios, Trilith Studios and Assembly Studios — that rival Los Angeles market in scale and amenities. I have worked closely with many of these facilities as they grew from concept to world-class campuses, and I can attest to their capacity to support the most demanding productions." Weizenecker said production tax incentives often serve as the "decisive tipping point" once the infrastructure boxes are checked. CARRIE UNDERWOOD SAYS HER FAMILY COULD BE 'SELF-SUSTAINED' ON TENNESSEE FARM AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD SPOTLIGHT "As someone instrumental in crafting the Georgia Entertainment Industry Investment Act, I have seen firsthand how Georgia's program offers structural advantages over California's that make it exceptionally attractive for a recurring, high-budget unscripted series." Additionally, Georgia has invested strategically in workforce development since the enactment of the Georgia Entertainment Industry Investment Act, according to Weizenecker. "The Georgia Film Academy, a collaboration among the University System of Georgia, the Technical College System of Georgia and the Georgia Department of Economic Development, has trained thousands of professionals across disciplines from grip and electric to visual effects. That pipeline, reinforced by the sheer volume of annual production activity, has created a self-sustaining ecosystem of IATSE-qualified crew members who live and work in the state full-time." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? "Post-production facilities offering editorial, color grading, sound mixing and VFX have expanded significantly, with several national and international post houses establishing Atlanta-area operations." "The same infrastructure supporting Marvel, Lucasfilm, Netflix and major network television productions is available to a show of 'American Idol's' caliber," he added. "Having advised many of the productions and facilities that anchor this ecosystem, I can confirm Georgia's vendor community is fully capable of supporting this show." The show’s relocation also underscores how its talent is already less tied to Los Angeles. Carrie Underwood, who won "American Idol" in 2005 and now serves as one of the show’s judges, has lived with her family on a 400-acre farm in Franklin, Tennessee, since leaving Hollywood in 2019. Underwood has described her Tennessee home as the place where she and her husband, former NHL player Mike Fisher, raise their two sons, care for livestock and grow vegetables. articles.title: 'Never complain, never explain': Buckingham Palace broke its own golden rule over Princess Diana claims
articles.summary: Buckingham Palace has taken the unusual step of challenging Earl Spencer's account of King Charles's reaction to Princess Diana's death.
articles.body:
Britain's royal family has taken the unusual step of publicly challenging claims made by Princess Diana's brother, Earl Spencer, in his upcoming memoir.

Departing from the monarchy's traditional "never complain, never explain" approach, Buckingham Palace responded Wednesday to Spencer's recollection of a phone call between himself and King Charles, in the wake of Diana's death in 1997. According to Spencer, the call took place after Spencer objected to Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, walking behind their mother's coffin at her funeral.

In an excerpt from the book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister published by Britain's Daily Mail , Spencer wrote, "He unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough.'"

While the palace didn't directly address whether the comment was made, the statement questioned the reliability of Spencer's recollection, saying, "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss."

The statement echoes the palace's reaction to claims made by Harry and Meghan Markle during their 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey that an unnamed royal had made a remark about their son's skin color before he was born and that the monarchy failed to help a suicidal Meghan. A response issued on behalf of Queen Elizabeth II at that time said that "recollections may vary."

Royal correspondents described Wednesday's statement as highly unusual. Sky News's Laura Bundock called it "a really remarkable intervention" and a "very robust response" that is "beyond punchy." Bundock added that the royal family "simply cannot stay silent."

The BBC's former royal correspondent Jennie Bond described the statement as "'recollections may vary' with bells on. [It] suggests they are going to hit back on this," she said , adding, "It's a right mess."

What is the 'never complain, never explain' motto?

Rather than a formal palace rule, the "never complain, never explain" phrase is an unofficial code of conduct, often credited to the Victorian-era British prime minister Benjamin Disraeli. The saying was later linked to Elizabeth II's mother and subsequently became a mantra that Elizabeth herself followed. Britain's former monarch almost never responded to criticism, political disputes or reports about her family during her 70-year reign.

Charles has also stuck to the same approach and has not responded to Harry's 2023 memoir Spare , despite numerous allegations about Charles, Queen Camilla and William. Similarly, the palace declined to comment on Tom Bower's book Rebel Prince and Omid Scobie's 2023 book Endgame .

Harry commented on the phrase during a 2023 interview with CBS's 60 Minutes , claiming the reality was more complicated.

"The family motto is 'never complain, never explain,' but it's just a motto," he said. "[Buckingham Palace] will feed or have a conversation with a correspondent, and that correspondent will literally be spoon-fed information and write the story, and at the bottom of it, they will say they have reached out to Buckingham Palace for comment. But the whole story is Buckingham Palace commenting."

Katie Nicholl, a Vanity Fair correspondent and author of Uncensored Royals , explained why the royal family upheld the motto on most occasions. "Dignified silence is a tried and tested format," she told Time magazine in 2023. "...The palace is reluctant to engage at any level because once they do, it just fuels the narrative." She added, "The Queen only responded when she absolutely had to and it was often short and succinct."

When else has the royal family publicly defended itself?

Aside from the Oprah interview and Spencer's new memoir, the royal family has publicly responded on several other notable occasions.

After facing heavy criticism for not returning to London from the family's Balmoral Castle residence in Scotland immediately after Diana's death, the Queen eventually addressed the U.K. in an extraordinary live speech five days later. She referred to herself "as your Queen" and "a grandmother," paid tribute to Diana and said she had remained at Balmoral to help "William and Harry come to terms with the devastating loss that they and the rest of us have suffered."

Andrew attempted to explain his friendship with Jeffrey Epstein and rebut Virginia Giuffre's allegations. The BBC interview was met with intense criticism, and Andrew soon withdrew from royal duties.

In 2025, Buckingham Palace announced that Andrew had been stripped of his prince title and would be moving out of his Royal Lodge home in Windsor, England.

A statement from the palace read, "These censures are deemed necessary, notwithstanding the fact that [Andrew] continues to deny the allegations against him. Their Majesties wish to make clear that their thoughts and utmost sympathies have been, and will remain with, the victims and survivors of any and all forms of abuse."

Bullying accusations against Meghan, 2021

After The Times of London reported that some former staff members had accused Meghan of bullying, the palace said it was "clearly very concerned" and said its HR team would look into how the complaints were handled. Meghan's representatives denied the allegations.

The Princes and the Press documentary, 2021

The three main royal households — Buckingham Palace (which represents the British monarch), Clarence House (Charles's home and communications team) and Kensington Palace (William and Kate's London office and household base) — joined forces to issue a rare rebuttal to a BBC documentary about William and Harry's relationship with the media, calling claims "overblown and unfounded."

The royal aide sparked uproar after repeatedly asking Ngozi Fulani, the founder and chief executive of a U.K. domestic abuse charity, where she "really" came from at a palace reception. Buckingham Palace called the comments "unacceptable and deeply regrettable." Hussey subsequently stepped aside from her honorary role the same day.

Buckingham Palace responded to allegations made by Harry after he lost an appeal over his U.K. security arrangements. Harry said the process had been used to control him and that the royal household had influenced the decision. The palace responded, "All of these issues have been examined repeatedly and meticulously by the courts, with the same conclusion reached on each occasion."

articles.title: Spotify’s Fresh Finds Forward gives artists free studio time and more
articles.summary: Spotify is providing emerging artists with a ton of resources, including free therapy.
articles.body: Getting added to Spotify’s Fresh Finds playlists can be a huge break for artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming. Now Spotify is launching a program called Fresh Finds Forward, which aims to give artists the tools to capitalize on that exposure. Artists added to any Fresh Finds playlist after January 1st, 2026, can join the program and get 12 months of additional resources, the most extravagant of which is free studio time for US-based artists at Electric Lady Studios in NYC, The Lighthouse at Ocean Way Nashville, or Spotify Studios in LA. Beyond that, artists will get early access to Spotify tools and features, priority access to tour and music video partnerships, as well as 12 months of Landr Studio Pro and Splice’s Creator Plan. Spotify is also offering artists six months of free therapy through BetterHelp, because we all know trying to make it as a musician is stressful and potentially soul-crushing, as scoring a Fresh Finds placement doesn’t guarantee there won’t be further rejections and failures. Unlike with the so-called Discovery Mode, where artists were paid a “promotional royalty rate,” in exchange for higher algorithmic promotion, Spotify says the Fresh Finds Forward program doesn’t change royalty rates, and is provided completely free of charge to participating artists.

articles.title: Irlanda comunica que no participará en Eurovisión en apoyo a Palestina
articles.standfirst: Segunda nación, junto a Países Bajos, que confirma su ausencia para la edición de 2027
articles.summary: Segunda nación, junto a Países Bajos, que confirma su ausencia para la edición de 2027
articles.body: Eurovisión pasa por una de sus crisis más graves en los últimos años al ver como cada vez son más los países participantes que se niegan a concursar en él ni a hacerles publicidad. El último caso ha sido el de Irlanda. La cadena pública irlandesa (RTE) mantiene su boicot al concurso y ha confirmado este jueves, 17 de septiembre, en un comunicado que no participará ni emitirá el Festival de Eurovisión 2027 que se celebra en Brujas el próximo mes de mayo, La RTE ha explicado en el escrito que su posición al respecto “se mantiene sin cambios”. “RTE considera que la participación de Irlanda no se justifica dada la terrible y continua pérdida de vidas en Gaza y la crisis humanitaria que sigue poniendo en riesgo la vida de tantos civiles. Así mismo, RTE sigue profundamente preocupada por la constante negativa a conceder acceso independiente a periodistas internacionales al territorio”, señalan en el comunicado. Esta será pues la segunda vez en la que Irlanda no participe, pues ya lo hizo este año por el mismo motivo. En especial, al considerar “grave” que la Unión Europea de Radiodifusión (UER) permitiera la participación de la israelí KAN. La República de Irlanda fue uno de los cinco países, junto con Islandia, Países Bajos, España y Eslovenia, que no participaron. Hasta la fecha solo los irlandeses y Países Bajos han confirmado que volverán a ausentarse de este certamen. Mientras países como la República de Irlanda o Países Bajos han confirmado que no estarán en el Festival de Eurovisión 2027, España sigue sin saber qué hará. Radio Televisión Española confirmó el año pasado que mientras Israel continúe participando, ellos no estarán. Lo que se presupone que dará pie a una nueva ausencia de los españoles.

articles.title: Singer Duncan Sheik in ‘critical but stable’ condition and receiving care
articles.summary: Tony Award-winning singer and songwriter Duncan Sheik is in “critical but stable” condition and receiving medical care, according to a statement posted to his Instagram account Wednesday evening.
articles.body: Tony Award-winning singer and songwriter Duncan Sheik is in “critical but stable” condition and receiving medical care, according to a statement posted to his Instagram account Wednesday evening. “Duncan is currently receiving medical care and remains in critical but stable condition,” the statement said. “Out of respect for Duncan and our family, we will not be sharing further medical details at this time,” it added. “We kindly ask for privacy during this incredibly difficult time and will provide updates when appropriate,” the statement continued. “Thank you for the continued love and support.” It remains unclear where Sheik is receiving medical care or what his prognosis is. Sheik, 56, is perhaps best known for his 1996 hit “Barely Breathing,” which remains at the top of his Spotify page three decades later. The song earned him a Grammy nomination for best male pop vocal performance. He has released nine studio albums over his career, with the most recent in 2022. In 2002, Sheik began writing music for the theater. That year, he composed the music for the New York Shakespeare Festival production of “Twelfth Night.” But his biggest break came just years later, in 2006, with the success of “Spring Awakening” on Broadway, for which he co-wrote the music with Steven Sater. His work on the breakout Broadway show earned him two Tony Awards: best orchestrations and best original score, which he shared with Sater. “Spring Awakening” also won best musical at the Tonys that year and earned a Grammy Award for best musical show album. According to a 2012 Broadway World article, Sheik said he had been working on the music for a “Spring Awakening” film adaptation. It is unclear whether that project is still in the works. The show’s off-Broadway revival begins previews on Nov. 27 and officially opens on Dec. 17. Sheik kept composing for the theater after “Spring Awakening,” writing music for “Alice By Heart” (2012), “American Psycho” (2013), “The Taming of the Shrew” (2016) and “The Secret Life of Bees” (2019).

articles.body: Over the years, many celebrities have revealed all kinds of odd hobbies and habits they have developed over the years. articles.title: Lunacy Audio Nova is a place to build and sell your own AI-powered music plug-ins
articles.summary: Lunacy Audio’s Nova is a plug-in for your DAW, a VST development platform, and a storefront for selling your AI-assisted creations.
articles.body: Lunacy, purveyor of fine VST plug-ins like Cube, a synth that you control by moving a ball around a 3D space, has just launched Nova, a platform where creators can build custom music tools using AI and sell them to others. At first, there will be a handful of instruments available, built either by Lunacy or a small selection of partner developers. But eventually, the company will launch Nova Builder, which will let anyone build their own plug-ins or remix existing ones. There are 10 plug-ins available initially, covering everything from crunchy chiptunes to warbly vintage synths and evil ambient drones. None of them do anything particularly unique, but they all sound pretty solid. The lo-fi Drift Cassette synth and Silhouettes are my two favorites right off the bat. The former gets you nostalgic ’80s tones, while the latter is all about sci-fi soundscapes. They all have pretty simple interfaces reminiscent of Native Instruments’ Play series, with bright colors and a handful of controls. What makes Nova different is that plug-ins aren’t built using code in a text editor. Instead, they’re assembled using premade effects blocks and AI prompts. It’s not unlike Polyend’s Endless, except instead of vibe-coding a guitar pedal, you’re creating music software anyone can use on their computer. Nova instruments don’t require dedicated hardware. Heck, they don’t even require a digital audio workstation (DAW) and can run directly in a browser. That’s of limited use, though. So there’s also a Nova host plug-in that runs in your DAW of choice. It lets you browse and load any Nova plug-in from your library and swap between them quickly. Lunacy envisions Nova as a tinkerers’ paradise. Cofounder and CEO Casey Kolb said in a press release that, “Say someone makes a step sequencer and shares it. You open it and wish you could add a custom shimmer reverb to the end of the signal chain. You can add that, then you can share your new version with a friend, and that friend expands it further. The tools are never fixed; they are always evolving.” So far, though, the response from the music-making community to AI has been rather tepid. Tools like Endless have been met with, at best, cautious curiosity, and at worst, outright hostility. Lunacy is developing Nova out in the open, posting developer diaries and actively seeking customer input, in an attempt to avoid some of the same pitfalls and win over wary musicians.

articles.title: In 1993, Michael Jackson, along with two collaborators, patented the ‘anti-gravity’ shoes; here's how the King of Pop pulled off his impossible-looking lean
articles.summary: Discover the engineering genius behind Michael Jackson's gravity-defying dance move in 'Smooth Criminal' through his patented anti-gravity shoes and stage mechanism.
articles.body: Michael Jackson had a way of making a dance move look like something the human body simply should not be able to do. One of the best examples came in 'Smooth Criminal', when the singer appeared to bend his body sharply forward while keeping his feet planted on the floor. For years, the move looked like a piece of stage magic. However, there was very real engineering behind it.Jackson, along with Michael L. Bush and Dennis Tompkins, was named as an inventor on a US patent that described a specially designed shoe and stage mechanism capable of producing the effect. The patent was filed in 1992 and granted the following year under the title 'Method and Means for Creating Anti-Gravity Illusion'. The patent record lists Triumph International, Inc. as the assignee.The patent behind Michael Jackson's gravity-defying moveThe details are laid out in U.S. Patent No. 5,255,452. According to the patent document, the invention was intended to create an "anti-gravity illusion" for entertainment. It wasn't designed to cancel gravity or make the performer weightless. Instead, it provided an additional point of support that allowed the performer to lean much farther forward than would normally be possible.The patent describes specialised footwear that could connect to a movable hitch or post built into the stage. When the mechanism was raised, the heel of the shoe could lock onto it. This gave the performer the support needed to shift his body forward and place his centre of gravity beyond the front of his shoes.The patent's inventors were Michael J. Jackson, Michael L. Bush and Dennis Tompkins. It was filed on June 29, 1992 and officially granted on October 26, 1993.What was hidden underneath the heels?The clever part of the design was inside the heel.The patent describes a recess in the heel that could receive the stage hitch. A V-shaped slot acted as a guide, allowing the heel to slide into position and engage with the protruding mechanism. Once connected, the shoe could remain firmly attached to the stage while Jackson leaned forward.The footwear was also designed to look relatively ordinary from an audience's perspective. The patent explains that parts of the shoe could be covered with material such as a sock section, spats or trouser legs. This helped conceal the unusual construction and allowed the footwear to blend into the performer's costume.The stage mechanism itself was designed to disappear when it wasn't needed. According to the patent, the hitch could move between a raised position and a retracted position, allowing the performer to dance normally before and after the move.Why couldn't ordinary shoes do the same thing?A normal pair of dance shoes would not have provided the necessary connection to the stage.The patented footwear contained a specially constructed heel, while the stage had corresponding hitch points that could rise through openings in the floor. The patent describes the hitch as being operated from beneath the stage, although it also discusses the possibility of remote-controlled operation.The design also addressed a problem with an earlier method of creating similar leaning effects. The patent notes that cables attached to a harness had previously been used for performers in recorded videos. However, such cables could restrict movement and required stage personnel to connect and disconnect them.The shoe-and-hitch arrangement offered a different solution. The performer could move around the stage and engage with the mechanism only when the dramatic lean was required.Was the ‘Smooth Criminal’ lean originally performed with these shoes?The patent itself provides useful context here. It explains that performers had already used cables and harnesses to create a similar forward-leaning effect in recorded performances. The invention was intended to make such a movement more practical for live entertainment.That distinction matters. The patent did not claim to invent gravity-defying movement itself. Instead, it described a particular mechanical system for reproducing the visual effect on stage.That is also why calling the footwear "anti-gravity shoes" can be slightly misleading. The phrase comes from the patent's title, but the document repeatedly describes the invention as an illusion created through footwear and stage hardware.What happened to the patent?The patent record shows that U.S. Patent No. 5,255,452 was granted on October 26, 1993. The current Google Patents record lists its legal status as "Expired - Fee Related," while also noting that its legal-status information is an assumption and not a legal conclusion.More than three decades after the patent was granted, the technology remains an interesting example of how entertainment and engineering can overlap. Jackson's famous lean may have looked supernatural to the audience, but beneath his heels was a carefully designed mechanical solution.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: In 1994, Brad Pitt bought a $1.7 million Los Feliz house; nearly 30 years later, the Hollywood compound sold for $39 million
articles.summary: Explore how Brad Pitt transformed a $1.7 million house into a sprawling $39 million compound in Los Feliz, showcasing luxury, family life, and architectural beauty over nearly three decades.
articles.body: Brad Pitt's long relationship with one Los Angeles address began in 1994, when he paid $1.7 million for a Craftsman-style house in Los Feliz. The actor bought the property from Cassandra Peterson, the actress widely known for playing Elvira. What started as a single historic house eventually became much larger as Pitt gradually acquired neighbouring parcels and reshaped the grounds around his original purchase.The Los Angeles Times reported in April 2023 that Pitt sold the longtime holding for $39 million. The transaction was completed just before a new Los Angeles transfer tax took effect, allowing the actor to avoid an additional $2.145 million tax bill on the sale.The 1915 Craftsman house that Brad Pitt bought in 1994At the heart of the Los Feliz holding was a Craftsman-style house built in 1915. The roughly 6,700-square-foot structure sat on a private knoll close to the boundary between Los Feliz and the Hollywood Hills.The Los Angeles Times reported that the original dwelling was surrounded by lush gardens and included six bedrooms and seven bathrooms. Outdoor features eventually included multiple pools, a koi pond and a skate park, giving the grounds a very different character from the single house Pitt had acquired almost three decades earlier.Peterson later provided a more personal account of the original transaction. In an exclusive interview with People, she recalled selling the house to Pitt in 1994 and telling him about what she believed were unusual experiences there. According to her account, the stories actually increased his interest in the place rather than discouraging him.How Brad Pitt expanded the Los Angeles holdingPitt's real-estate plans did not stop with the first purchase. The Los Angeles Times reported that he acquired four surrounding properties between 1998 and 2009.Those additional purchases gradually increased the amount of land under his control to roughly two acres. Instead of one standalone residence, the actor had created a secluded setting assembled over many years.The process also produced an unexpected connection with one of the neighbouring occupants. Peterson told People that one of the houses Pitt acquired belonged to an elderly man named John. Rather than asking him to move, Pitt allowed him to remain there without paying rent.According to Peterson, John eventually lived until the age of 105. She described the arrangement as an example of Pitt's kindness toward the longtime occupant.Inside Brad Pitt's longtime family settingThe Los Feliz address was not simply a place Pitt kept as an investment. It became closely connected to his family life.During his relationship with Angelina Jolie, the couple lived there with their six children. People reported that the residence was where the family raised Maddox, Pax, Zahara, Shiloh, Knox and Vivienne.The size of the surrounding grounds gave the family considerable privacy. Gardens and recreational facilities provided space away from the busy streets of Los Angeles, while the location offered access to the city's entertainment industry.The main structure also retained architectural details that reflected its age. Architectural Digest has highlighted features associated with the Craftsman-style dwelling, including mahogany panelling and copper ceilings, which contributed to its period character.Gardens, pools and a private outdoor worldAs Pitt expanded the surrounding land, the outdoor areas became an important part of the overall setting.According to the Los Angeles Times, the grounds included lush gardens, a koi pond, a skate park and multiple pools. These additions gave the nearly two-acre setting a resort-like quality while preserving the privacy that had made the location attractive in the first place.The landscaping also helped separate the house from the surrounding neighbourhood. Rather than being dominated by a large building, the setting incorporated substantial greenery around the structures.That combination of historic architecture and extensive outdoor space gave the Los Feliz holding an identity of its own. It was not simply a conventional celebrity mansion but a collection of spaces that had developed gradually over Pitt's years of ownership.Brad Pitt sold the house for $39 million in 2023After nearly three decades, Pitt decided to sell the Los Angeles holding. The transaction was handled privately rather than through a conventional public listing.The Los Angeles Times reported that the property was quietly offered to potential buyers for around $40 million. Because it was a pocket listing, detailed information and photographs were not widely circulated before the deal closed.The final figure came to $39 million, with the sale completed in the closing days of March 2023. The timing was significant because Los Angeles' new Measure ULA transfer tax took effect on April 1. At that price, the tax would have added approximately $2.145 million to the transaction had the deal closed after the deadline.For years, the address also served as a family setting, marking an important period in Pitt's personal life. Eventually, however, the actor moved on from the Los Feliz holding. What began with a $1.7 million purchase in 1994 ended with a $39 million private sale in 2023. Between those two figures lies nearly three decades of gradual expansion from one 1915 Craftsman house to a secluded Los Angeles compound spanning roughly two acres.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Eva Shockey says women don't have to abandon their femininity to belong in the outdoors
articles.summary: Eva Shockey reveals the hunting community's pushback she faced for looking feminine and why she refused to change who she is to fit the mold.
articles.body: Eva Shockey never thought becoming a hunter should require giving up the other parts of herself. Apparently, plenty of people disagreed. Shockey, one of the most recognizable women in the outdoor industry, told OutKick's Tomi Lahren that she has faced pushback from within the hunting community almost from the moment she entered it — including criticism for something as simple as wanting to look feminine while doing it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS "Pretty much everything I've done in the hunting community, there's been pushback since day one," Shockey said during an appearance on "Tomi Lahren is Fearless." "It's never been where everyone's like, 'Yeah, she's doing it right.' Like, it's just never been like that." But fitting neatly into someone else's idea of what a hunter should look like was never particularly appealing to her. Shockey grew up in a hunting family as the daughter of legendary outdoorsman Jim Shockey, but she didn't immediately follow her dad into the field. In fact, one of the things that kept her away from hunting when she was younger was that she didn't see women who looked or lived like her doing it. When she eventually began hunting herself, she wasn't interested in trading one identity for another. "I didn't hunt because I didn't know you could be this — have hair and makeup and care about your nails being done — and also love to hunt," she said. "I love being in the mountains. I love hiking. I love wearing camo, but I also like still looking feminine." Her solution was pretty simple: Don't choose. "If I'm gonna hunt, I'm still me," Shockey said. "I'm not gonna change who I am because I want to go hunting." STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW! That became a defining part of her message as her profile grew over the years. Shockey came into the outdoor industry at a time when hunting media was still overwhelmingly male. She started on television alongside her father before social media opened the door for women and other newcomers to find outdoor personalities who looked more like them. She is quick to point out that she didn't create the movement toward more women hunting. "I got to really ride the wave of a big change in more women starting to hunt," Shockey said. "It wasn't me personally. Like, no, I'm not going to take all that credit. There was a bunch of other women before me. I just got to be a bit of a face of it and represent a lot of women through those last 15 years or so." Still, she has seen the change firsthand. Shockey believes social media, for all its faults, has made the outdoor world far more accessible to girls who might otherwise grow up believing hunting simply isn't something women do. "If young girls want to see someone shooting a bow or they live out in the country and they've never seen a girl hunt — which was little Eva back in the day — they can open social and see people doing what they want to do," she said. And they don't all have to look the same. "I'm by no means everybody's style," Shockey said. "Not everyone wants to see someone with, like, hair and makeup done. But there's lots." That's precisely the point. For Shockey, expanding hunting isn't about replacing one stereotype with another. It's about showing women that they don't have to adopt a particular personality, appearance or identity before they're allowed to participate. CHASE BRISCOE SAYS DEER HUNTING GIVES HIM A BIGGER RUSH THAN DRIVING 200 MPH IN NASCAR Over the years, she said, that message has come back to her directly. "I had a lot of girls, thousands and thousands of girls over the years, come up to me with basically relaying that to me," Shockey said. "Like, 'I'm so glad you said that we could hunt and not be embarrassed of who we are or what we look like or where we're from or whatever that looks like.'" And it isn't necessarily about makeup or femininity. "Maybe it's not hair and makeup," she said. "It's just you want to be who you are and still enjoy hunting. You don't have to transition into a hunter and leave everything else out. Like, we all have more elements than that." Shockey also believes the broader culture has moved closer to the outdoor lifestyle in recent years. More people, she said, are showing interest in gardening, sourcing their own food, hunting and generally reconnecting with where food comes from. "It's changed a lot in the last five years," she said. "I think people are very interested in that lifestyle, and they're very interested in growing things themselves, hunting things themselves." Rather than policing exactly how deeply someone participates, Shockey would rather see that curiosity encouraged. "The things that I believe so strongly in — like the outdoor life, the hunting, the gardens, the healthy food for your family, the fresh air, all that — I believe it's such a great thing," she said. "Even if they're doing 10% of it, that's 10% better than not doing it." And for Shockey, that may be the bigger win. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Not everyone has to become a hardcore hunter. But if seeing women with different personalities, interests and backgrounds makes the outdoors feel a little less foreign — and a little more accessible — then she’s certainly done her job. articles.title: Matthew Lillard ‘ashamed’ he returned to ‘Scream’ franchise after Melissa Barrera fired for Israel-Gaza posts
articles.summary: Matthew Lillard expressed regret on Tuesday over his decision to film “Scream 7” after actor Melissa Barrera was fired from the franchise over her social media about the Israel-Gaza war, saying he was “on the wrong side of history.”
articles.body: Matthew Lillard expressed regret on Tuesday over his decision to film “Scream 7” after actor Melissa Barrera was fired from the franchise over her social media about the Israel-Gaza war, saying he was “on the wrong side of history.” Video showed the actor speaking to fans during a Q&A at a 30th anniversary screening for the original “Scream” at a Regal movie theater in Austin, Texas. It’s unclear what the question was, as the video only shows Lillard speaking, but it appears to be related to celebrities taking stances on political topics. Lillard described it as a “great question” and referred to the ongoing situation with singer Ed Sheeran, who is facing backlash after venues pressured him to drop Macklemore from his tour over his pro-Palestinian remarks. “I don’t think it’s easy all the time,” he said, before referring to Barrera. Barrera starred in “Scream 6” and was expected to return for the seventh installment of the hit horror franchise, but was fired in 2023. Spyglass Media Group, the production company behind the film, confirmed it had dropped Barrera after she shared Instagram posts condemning Israel. According to a Variety report, Barrera’s post included references to Israel as a “colonized” land and reshared posts that accused Israel of “genocide and ethnic cleansing.” Another post said that “Western media only shows the (Israeli) side.” “Why do they do that, I will let you deduce for yourself,” the post reportedly said. Spyglass Media Group told Variety in a statement that it has zero tolerance for “antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form.” Barrera initially declined to comment, but later told the Associated Press that she was “grateful” for everything that had happened and felt it was an “awakening.” “Melissa Barrera, who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said after the whole Palestinian— what started happening in Israel,” Lillard said. “It’s really f---ing bulls--- and really hard and she’s on the right side of history.” “But the whole world should have popped up and said, ‘She’s right.’ And they didn’t. And that’s brutal,” he said. The “Scream” actor’s remarks come days after rapper Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran’s tour over a speech and performance centered on his pro-Palestinian views. Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, said Monday that venues threatened to cancel Sheeran’s shows in response to the rapper saying “Free Palestine” on stage. Among those involved was New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who Macklemore accused of organizing a boycott against the rapper. While talking about the consequences Barrerra suffered, Lillard said, “And when they start coming after your job, sometimes things are worth it.” He noted that he “got called out” for returning to the “Scream” franchise in the same film Barrera was set to star in. Lillard described himself as being on “the wrong side of history” for that choice. “I feel bad about that, I feel ashamed about that,” Lillard said. “Because in that moment I was so excited to go back that I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey and didn’t say no. And I’m embarrassed, and that’s the truth.” “I still like being in the movie, but it may not have been the best idea,” he said.

articles.title: Best hikes in and around Oxford to get you ready for Ole Miss-LSU's week three showdown
articles.summary: From Sardis Lake's 13-mile Clear Creek Trail to the family-friendly Lamar Park walking loop, these Oxford hikes are perfect before Ole Miss vs. LSU.
articles.body: The eyes of the college football world will be focused this weekend on Oxford, Mississippi, for the showdown between Ole Miss and LSU. Two top-ten teams in the SEC duking it out is already newsworthy, but with the added context of Tigers coach Lane Kiffin making his way back to Vaught Hemingway Stadium for the first time since his departure from the university, this one is sure to be a hot ticket. If you're lucky enough to be attending the game, you'll likely want to enjoy the great outdoors and take in all the natural beauty that the Magnolia State has to offer, and luckily for you, we here at OutKick OutDoors have you covered. BEST HIKES TO TRY AROUND LUBBOCK AHEAD OF TEXAS TECH'S WEEK ONE MATCHUP WITH ABILENE CHRISTIAN Here are four of the best hikes in and around Oxford to help you usher in the game on Saturday. South Campus Rail Trail For those of you wanting a real hike without ever leaving the friendly confines of Oxford, this one is an absolute slam dunk. The South Campus Rail Trail features a five-mile round trip trail that follows an old gravel railroad bed (hence the name), while the surrounding network contains more than 20 miles of single-track trails, according to the university website. It's right by campus so you don't have to travel too far, and it also features a quiet, wooded area to take your mind off the stresses of gameday. Whether you're looking for a straightforward walk or something a little more adventurous through the surrounding woods, South Campus Rail Trail is the move. Clear Creek Trail at Sardis Lake Serious hikers who actually came to work up a sweat will love Clear Creek Trail. It's a little further away - about 30 minutes from downtown Oxford - but the drive is well worth it. Clear Creek Trail offers a 13-mile loop around nearby Sardis Lake, and the trails are even split up for different levels of hikers. There's a three-mile beginner loop or an eight-mile beginner/intermediate combination, meaning there's something for everyone. The views of the lake are spectacular, especially during late summer and early fall, and the proximity to the water means hikers can make a full outdoors day that includes a little fishing if you've come prepared. 6 OF THE BEST FALL CAMPING DESTINATIONS IN AMERICA, PLUS GEAR BEGINNERS SHOULD PACK One thing to note is that this doubles as a mountain biking trail, so hikers should be aware of this and yield appropriately. The combo of the woods and the water make this a must-see. Holly Springs National Forest It's been called the antithesis of a college football Saturday, and although that sounds like a pejorative, I can assure you it's not. Holly Springs National Forest is probably the most secluded and serene spot on this list, so if you really just need to get away from it all before a stressful slate of SEC football, this is the place for you. 14 TAILGATING ESSENTIALS FOR GRILLING, WATCHING THE GAME AND STAYING WARM The area offers a remote destination for hikers who don't want to deal with the large crowds some of the more "touristy" destinations hold. The whole forest is home to 155,000 acres of federal land, and a special mention needs to be made for the recreation area at Chewalla Lake, which is great for hiking, fishing, canoeing, and more. With it being so secluded, you'll have to drive a bit to get here (Google Maps plots it as 65 minutes from Oxford), but that's the price you pay for being one with nature. If you're looking to broaden your horizons and really explore everything northern Mississippi has to offer, make the trek here. You won't regret it. Lamar Park So, you brought the whole family along for a little SEC football action? Great! If you're looking for a hike you and the kids can enjoy, Lamar Park is the place to be. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! It's a six-minute car ride from the stadium, so you won't have to worry about entertaining the rugrats on a long road trip, and once you arrive, you'll find a well manicured park and a low intensity walking loop for hikers trying to avoid a more strenuous workout. Anyone who is trying to get a little sunshine and some fresh air on the morning of the game without busting their butt should check this place out, as it's more of a scenic stroll than a heart-racing romp through the wilderness. articles.title: Mackenzie Phillips makes new claims about father's alleged abuse
articles.summary: Mackenzie Phillips revealed a letter from a family friend corroborated her abuse claims against father John Phillips on Valerie Bertinelli's podcast.
articles.body: For decades, Mackenzie Phillips said she lived with the pain of not being believed about her late father, John Phillips. Then an unexpected letter landed in her hands – and changed everything. Phillips opened up about a stunning letter from a longtime family friend that corroborated her claims of abuse by her late father during an episode of Valerie Bertinelli's podcast, "Get Naked." Phillips recalled receiving the letter while working at Breathe Life Healing Center. MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SHOCKS WITH 15-YEAR CELIBACY CONFESSION AS SHARON STONE, TERI HATCHER RETHINK ROMANCE "Head of HR comes in. And he says, 'Oh, you got a letter.' And I said, 'Oh, wow. It's probably fan mail.' Because, you know, we get fan mail there," she told Bertinelli. "And I won't go into too much detail, but it was from one of the most credible sources you could ever know of a family friend saying that... their husband observed something horrific when I was 9." "And I said, ‘Jeffrey’ – my brother, you know – 'I want to tell you.' He said, 'I don't want to know.' Nobody wants to know. Nobody wants to know, you know," Mackenzie said. "So I'm on my own again... I'm on my own in this nobody believes me." "Here's the thing is that I told the people – that said that I was lying – back then," she added. "They already knew. But I got this letter." Bertinelli asked Mackenzie how it affected her to find the courage to speak out only to have people not believe her. MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SAYS SHE AND VALERIE BERTINELLI DRANK WINE, DID COCAINE DURING SITCOM BREAKS "Well, there's an element of protecting the legacy of The Mamas & The Papas," she explained. "I can separate the man from the music. I know that this was like the perfect storm of drugs and alcohol and untreated mental health. My dad was a not-well man." "But I got this letter, and I'm sitting there reading it, and it was like shocking, shocking – the content," Mackenzie recalled. "And this woman said, 'I'm so sorry I didn't come forward to support you while you were on "Oprah." I was afraid. I didn't know what to do. But here's what happened.' And I'm sitting there. And I'm like numb." At the time, Mackenzie had the director of Breathe Life Healing Center read the letter. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "And I handed it to her, and she sat in the chair in my office, and she went, 'Oh my God, Mac.' And tears started pouring down her face," she remembered. "I could feel nothing. I just sat." "But she said, 'Mac, honey, it's time. It's time for you to dig even deeper. It's time because now that you have this, you had a knowing all along, but now you have proof of being groomed from a very young age,'" Mackenzie recalled. Mackenzie alleged John had raped her at age 19 in her memoir, "High on Arrival," published in 2009. "I woke up that night from a blackout to find myself having sex with my own father," she wrote. "I don't remember how it started or, thankfully, how it ended." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS After the alleged rape, Mackenzie claimed the intimate relationship became consensual and lasted for 10 years before she became pregnant. The incest stopped then, and she had an abortion, according to Mackenzie's memoir. However, Mackenzie now views the relationship with her father differently. "I learned from my appearance on 'Oprah' and my book that – because I was calling it consensual because I was trying to protect him – there is no such thing as consent between a parent and a child,' she told Bertinelli. "The power differential is too great." John died in 2001 at the age of 65 after suffering from heart failure, years before Mackenzie's memoir was published. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Mackenzie's disclosure divided members of the Phillips family, although Mackenzie’s half-sister Chynna publicly supported her for speaking about her experience. John married four times and fathered five children: Jeffrey and Mackenzie with Susan Adams; Chynna Phillips with Michelle Phillips; and Tamerlane and Bijou Phillips with Geneviève Waïte. Known as "Papa John," the musician helped create the signature California folk-rock sound of the 1960s as a principal songwriter, singer and arranger for The Mamas & the Papas. Among the songs most closely associated with his songwriting are "California Dreamin,'" "Monday, Monday," "I Saw Her Again," "Creeque Alley" and "San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair)." articles.title: Barstool chief Dave Portnoy blasts Macklemore's shady past, strongly supports Patriots owner Robert Kraft
articles.summary: Dave Portnoy backed Robert Kraft's Gillette Stadium ban on Macklemore, slamming the rapper's antisemitic history and political rants on Ed Sheeran's tour.
articles.body: Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy firmly backed Patriots owner Robert Kraft’s decision to ban Macklemore from Gillette Stadium, telling the rapper to take his political activism somewhere else. Kraft’s decision helped get Macklemore kicked off Ed Sheeran’s U.S. "Loop Tour" after the Patriots owner cited the rapper’s history of antisemitic controversies. "I back Robert Kraft banning Macklemore from performing at Gillette 1000% and thank him for having a spine when many others in his shoes don't," Portnoy said in a video posted to X. MACKLEMORE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER GETTING KICKED OFF ED SHEERAN TOUR AFTER PRO-PALESTINE STANCE "Macklemore, who is turning this into a political rally, you're going to come into Bob Kraft's house and spit in his face? No f------ way!" Portnoy said. "That's not censorship. This ain't freedom of speech, homie. He owns the stadium! It's his house." He added: "Would you have a party and invite someone over who is going to spew what you consider hatred? If I go to the Ed Sheeran concert, I don't want to hear a ‘Free Palestine’ rant from a guy who isn't being genuine about it all. I didn't pay to hear Macklemore give me a political speech, I paid to hear Ed Sheeran sing." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Portnoy spotlighted Macklemore’s antisemitic past. "Bob Kraft, I am sure, did what I did when I saw this, he researched Macklemore," Portnoy said. "It didn't take long to learn that Macklemore has a pretty shady past. He already, at a prior concert, dressed in wildly antisemitic tropes." Portnoy was referring to a 2014 Seattle performance in which Macklemore wore a dark suit, fake beard and prosthetic nose, drawing criticism for invoking antisemitic Jewish caricatures. Macklemore later apologized. During Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and Sept. 5 shows at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, Macklemore led anti-Israel chants, projected Gaza war imagery and performed "Hind’s Hall." Several venues reportedly told the tour promoter they would not host shows if Macklemore remained on the lineup. Kraft refused to host him at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, and the promoter ultimately removed him from the remaining dates. Macklemore later accused Kraft of coordinating a stadium boycott against him. He pledged his $1 million in tour earnings to Palestinian aid and challenged Kraft to match the donation. In a statement released through Gillette Stadium, Kraft said Sheeran had contacted him privately before Macklemore’s public challenge. Sheeran asked Kraft to support a $2 million humanitarian donation, and Kraft said he agreed to support relief efforts in the region. Kraft also cited Macklemore’s history of antisemitic tropes and his failure to acknowledge the Oct. 7 Hamas attack that killed 1,200 people. PINK HITS BACK AMID BACKLASH FOR CRITICIZING MACKLEMORE'S PRO-PALESTINIAN CONCERT REMARKS After Macklemore was dropped, opening acts including Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga pulled out of the remaining tour dates in protest. Portnoy slammed the musicians who abandoned Sheeran’s tour, accusing them of hypocrisy and putting political posturing ahead of their commitment to fans. "I feel bad for Ed Sheeran; his band quit, saying, ‘This is censorship, Free Palestine!’ That guy, Finneas, the brother of Billie Eilish, f------ hypocrites; they backed out," Portnoy said. Portnoy closed by insisting that defending Kraft required more than a token show of support. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD "I don't stand with Bob Kraft 5 percent, 10 percent," Portnoy said. "I stand with Bob Kraft 110 percent. More Jews have to speak out. That's why I am making this video, because it's really easy for everyone just to pile on right now, but I have his back a hundred million percent." articles.title: María Valverde recuerda su vídeo viral sobre las relaciones sexuales en su anterior visita a 'La Revuelta': "La gente está enferma"
articles.standfirst: La actriz cerró una nueva semana en ‘La Revuelta’, de la 1 de RTVE
articles.summary: La actriz cerró una nueva semana en ‘La Revuelta’, de la 1 de RTVE
articles.body: ‘La Revuelta’ cerró una semana más este jueves, 17 de septiembre, en el ‘access prime time’ de La 1 de RTVE con David Broncano al frente. En esta entrega, la invitada al Teatro Albéniz fue María Valverde, reconocida actriz de nuestro país al aparecer en algunas ficciones como ‘Tres metros sobre el cielo’. La intérprete acudió al programa del canal del ente público a presentar su nuevo proyecto, una nueva miniserie llamada ‘El problema final’, adaptación de la novela de Arturo Pérez-Reverte, compuesta por 13 actores encerrados en un hotel y que llegará a Netflix el próximo día 25 de este mes. Así le dio la bienvenida el presentador: “Ya vino hace tiempo y es una gran actriz, que ganó un premio Goya con tan solo 16 años y por fin la tenemos aquí”. Valverde agradeció la calurosa bienvenida entre aplausos y vítores y tocó el bombo junto a Broncano nada más llegar. Posteriormente, charlaron de su anterior trabajo, en el que dedicó cuatro años de su vida y en el que se estrenó como directora: ‘El canto de las manos’, de ‘La flaqueza del bolchevique’ o ‘Tres metros sobre el cielo’, revelando que, aunque haya tenido papeles muy diferentes “no suele verse después”: “No todos los rodajes son una fantasía”, añadió. Luego, tuvo lugar el típico intercambio de regalos entre invitado y el comunicador del programa de La 1 de RTVE. De la misma manera, salió a relucir su lado personal, recalcando que quiere “seguir el camino” de sus abuelos, que son “maravillosos” y que aún le queda para ser una “anciana muy cuchi”. Broncano aprovechó para mandar un saludo a todos los abuelos y abuelas de nuestro país. Asimismo, la crítica salió a escena, pero se lo toma “con gracia” el ‘hate’ en comentarios, pero incidió en que tiene “buenos seguidores” y “cariñosos. Llegando al tramo final de la entrevista, Broncano recordó el momento viral que vivió Valverde por aquel entonces en ‘La Resistencia’ relacionado con las preguntas clásicas y que se hizo viral y que fue el más visto del programa en redes. Fue cuando el presentador le preguntó sobre las relaciones sexuales y ella dijo que había que masturbarse o mantener relaciones para “liberar oxitocina” y para disfrutar más el orgasmo. Aunque haya pasado el tiempo, no lo olvida, según reveló: “Calla, calla, no sé si quiero escucharte. El vídeo me persiguió mucho tiempo, la gente está enferma y no lo entendieron muy bien, ahí la mente de cada uno…”. Eso sí, en esta ocasión no respondió a ninguna, pero recalcó que le “iba muy bien en todo” para cerrar una nueva semana en ‘La Revuelta’ de La 1 de RTVE.
